opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to distinguish between different kinds of pauses, because their effects can be quite different and even opposite in sign.

The thing I'm most enthusiastic about is the ability to slow down or pause at the critical point, when we're getting to AI systems that can automate AI research itself and things could move from human-level to vastly superhuman capabilities in a year or two. That's when having extra time for safety work, for interpretability, for alignment evaluation, would be enormously valuable, and when a lot of that work could itself be done by AI systems we can actually study. Having the option to slow down then, ideally with international verification so that no one feels they're handing the lead to a rival, is extremely valuable.

A unilateral or voluntary pause now has a few problems. First, if it's only the more safety-conscious actors who pause, then you're selecting for leadership by the companies and countries that care less about these risks. The frontier shifts toward whoever is least willing to hold back, and the cautious actors lose influence over norms, standards, and the eventual deployment of the most powerful systems.

Second, there's the hardware overhang issue. If you stop training frontier models while chip production, algorithmic progress, and investment continue, then when the pause ends, or when someone defects, you get a sudden jump in capabilities rather than gradual progress. That's worse for safety, because you lose the incremental experience with each generation of systems and the chance to notice problems at lower stakes.

Third, there's a kind of political capital issue. If you spend a lot of credibility on a pause now, when systems aren't yet clearly dangerous, and it's seen as premature, that can make it harder to get coordinated action later when the evidence of danger is much stronger and a pause would buy much more.

So my view is less "pauses are bad" and more that we should be building the capacity for a well-timed, verifiable, multilateral slowdown: monitoring of compute, evaluations that tell us when we're approaching dangerous capabilities, agreements between the leading powers. That gets you the benefits of extra time at the moment it's most valuable, without the selection effects and overhang problems of a premature unilateral stop.

r001.rationale: It says spending credibility on a premature pause could make coordinated action harder later, when danger is clearer and a pause would be more valuable.

r002.rationale: It explains that if safety-conscious actors pause, leadership shifts toward companies and countries that care less about the risks.

r003.rationale: It describes continued chip production and a sudden capability jump after a pause, but does not say nonparticipating states would gain ground.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that an AI race leader could use its lead to spend more time on safety.

r005.rationale: It identifies AI systems automating AI research as the critical point for slowing progress and calls for an international, verified approach.

r006.rationale: It favors a verified multilateral slowdown over a unilateral stop, but does not specify a binding agreement backed by all great powers.

r007.rationale: It mentions compute monitoring and evaluations, but not mandatory reporting of powerful AI training or government intervention as danger emerges.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing to keep in mind is that a pause is only as good as what fills the time it buys. And a voluntary or unilateral pause doesn't actually buy time for the world; it buys time for everyone except the people who paused.

So suppose the most safety-conscious labs, the ones that have been thinking hardest about alignment and have the most internal pressure to do things carefully, decide to stop. The frontier doesn't stop. It just gets handed to whoever is next in line, and selection effects mean that's going to be actors who were less worried about these risks to begin with, or who are in a competitive position where they feel they can't afford to slow down. You've changed who's at the frontier, and in the direction of less caution, while barely changing when the frontier arrives. If you're a few months ahead and you pause, the thing you've done is remove a few months of lead time that could have been spent on safety work at the point where it actually matters, which is on the most capable systems.

And that's the second issue. A lot of the safety work that I think is most valuable is not something you can do in isolation from capabilities. You need the strong models to study them: to see what deceptive behaviour actually looks like, to test interpretability tools against systems that are smart enough to be dangerous, to practise the kinds of oversight we'd want to apply. If the careful groups pause and the less careful groups keep building, then the people with the data and the systems are not the people doing the research. So you've reduced the amount of safety-relevant work, not increased it.

Then there's the geopolitical version, which is really the same logic one level up. If one country pauses and its rivals don't, you've shifted the relative balance of this technology toward whoever didn't pause. And if you think about what the worst outcomes look like, a lot of them involve a single actor, whether a state or a lab or the AI systems themselves, getting a decisive advantage with nobody able to check it. A unilateral pause by the more scrupulous party makes that more likely, not less.

Now, I want to be clear that none of this is an argument against slowing down as such. If you could get a coordinated, enforceable, global agreement, with verification, with compute monitoring, so that everyone really did stop at the same time and the breathing room was shared, I think that could be enormously valuable. The thing I'm skeptical of is the version where you hope that by stepping back yourself, others will follow out of goodwill. The incentives mostly run the other way. Your stepping back makes racing more attractive for the others, because the prize gets closer.

So my view is that effort is better spent on the things that make coordination possible: building verification capacity, getting governments the technical competence to actually regulate, developing the evaluations that would let you say "this system is too dangerous to deploy" in a way that's credible to others. Those are things that could make a real pause work later. A unilateral pause mostly just trades away the influence you'd need to make that happen.

r001.rationale: It says a unilateral pause could trade away influence needed to make a later coordinated pause work, but does not identify losing the ability to pause later when stakes are higher.

r002.rationale: It says if the most safety-conscious labs pause, the frontier shifts to actors who are less concerned about the risks, increasing their relative position.

r003.rationale: It says rival states could gain relative advantage if one country pauses, but does not identify continued semiconductor or computing infrastructure development as the mechanism.

r004.rationale: It explains that pausing while a few months ahead gives up lead time that could have been spent on safety work with the most capable systems.

r005.rationale: It does not mention the point when AI fully automates AI research or identify that period as especially important for international regulation of progress.

r006.rationale: It calls a coordinated, enforceable global agreement valuable and contrasts it with a unilateral pause that shifts incentives toward racing.

r007.rationale: It mentions verification, compute monitoring, and evaluations, but not mandatory reporting of powerful AI training that lets governments intervene as danger emerges.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot depends on who’s pausing and what happens during the pause. Slowing down development isn’t automatically the same thing as improving our position. You want the extra time to produce more progress on safety, better institutions, and a greater ability to coordinate. And you have to compare that with what everyone else is doing during that period.

If the people most concerned about safety voluntarily stop, while less cautious developers continue, you can change who gets to the frontier. You may give up a lead that would otherwise let you invest more in safety or accept some delay without being overtaken. And if the pause is unilateral at the level of a country, there’s a similar concern: you could shift influence over how advanced AI is deployed toward a government that handles those decisions worse.

There’s also the question of what safety work you can do in the meantime. Some of it can happen independently of frontier development. But some requires access to the systems you’re trying to understand, and some could be greatly accelerated by more capable AI assistants. So you shouldn’t count every additional year as a year of safety progress while holding all the other consequences fixed.

That’s different from an enforceable international agreement that actually constrains the relevant actors, includes monitoring, and uses the time for concrete safety measures. There could be a strong case for that. My skepticism is about treating a voluntary or unilateral pause as though it delivers those benefits without the coordination problem. You need a story about why the pause changes the eventual outcome for the better, rather than just changing the date or who develops the technology first.

r001.rationale: The response discusses losing a lead and changing who develops first, but does not say an early pause could weaken the ability to pause later when stakes are higher.

r002.rationale: It says that if the most safety-conscious developers stop while less cautious developers continue, who reaches the frontier—and thus who has influence—can change.

r003.rationale: It discusses a country pausing and shifting influence to another government, but does not identify nonparticipating states gaining ground through semiconductor or computing infrastructure development.

r004.rationale: It says giving up a lead could mean losing the ability to invest more in safety or tolerate delays without being overtaken.

r005.rationale: The response does not identify full automation of AI research as a particularly important point for regulating the pace of progress.

r006.rationale: It favors an enforceable international agreement over a voluntary or unilateral pause, but does not specify that all great powers must back the agreement.

r007.rationale: The response mentions monitoring, but not mandatory reporting of powerful AI training or government intervention as evidence of imminent danger emerges.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what happens during the pause, and who is participating. A pause is useful to the extent that it changes the situation we’ll face when development resumes: we have better safety techniques, better institutions, or a stronger ability to prevent reckless deployment. Merely moving the date back doesn’t necessarily do that.

And a voluntary pause by the most safety-conscious developers has a particular problem: it can shift the lead to developers who are less concerned about safety. If one company stops while others continue, you haven’t necessarily reduced the danger. You may have reduced the influence of the people who were most willing to take precautions.

There’s also a distinction between stopping the development of more capable systems and stopping the activities that generate useful evidence about how to make them safe. Some safety work can be done with existing systems, but some depends on studying the capabilities and failure modes that emerge as systems become more powerful. So you need an account of which activities you’re stopping and which you’re trying to accelerate.

That doesn’t mean a pause could never help. A sufficiently broad, enforceable agreement, tied to concrete safety requirements and a serious programme of research and preparation, could be valuable. But that’s quite different from asking a few willing actors to stand still and hoping the rest of the world uses the extra time well.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether a pause improves conditions when development resumes, but does not say it could make a later pause harder when the stakes are higher.

r002.rationale: It says a pause by the most safety-conscious developers could shift the lead and reduce the influence of those most willing to take precautions.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss nonparticipating states gaining ground through semiconductor or computing infrastructure development.

r004.rationale: It mentions a shift in the lead but does not explain that a substantial lead gives its holder more time to work on safety.

r005.rationale: It does not identify AI automating AI research as a particularly important point for international regulation.

r006.rationale: It favors a broad, enforceable agreement over a pause by a few willing actors, but does not specify an agreement backed by all great powers.

r007.rationale: It does not discuss mandatory reporting of powerful AI training or government intervention as danger emerges.
